author: Codex socialist_green assessment agent (AI-assisted independent assessment)
changeNote: Completed 240 individually interpreted responses and separate substantive evidence review. User authorised neutral representative doctrinal modelling; no 12Axes answers or scores imported.

metadata.name: Green Politics
metadata.description: Democratic ecological politics in the Global Greens Charter tradition, combining ecological limits, social justice, diversity and grassroots participation.
metadata.period: Global Greens Charter, 2017 edition; implementation context checked October 2026
metadata.scope: Democratic ecological politics in the retrieved 2017 Global Greens Charter, including ecological limits, social justice, diversity, grassroots democracy and nonviolence. This excludes eco-authoritarianism. Recent EU ecological legislation is a real institutional application and compromise, not evidence that the EU or its incumbent governments embody the whole doctrine. This is a representative interpretation, not a questionnaire submitted by adherents. Numeric neutral means a stated mixed/conditional judgement, including rejection of the premise where explained; it is not a claim of measured empirical equivalence. Modern biological and technology items are conditional interpretive judgements where no exact historical position exists; they must not be read as empirical findings or a representative survey of adherents.
metadata.phrase: A democratic society living within ecological limits while pursuing social justice, nonviolence and shared responsibility.

sources.title: Environmental Ethics, including social ecology and competing environmental philosophies
Nature restoration law: Council gives final green light
Nature Restoration Regulation: current implementation overview
EU countries submit draft plans on restoring nature

axes.brief: The Charter requires equal adult voting, multiparty participation, transparency and grassroots democratic influence.
axes.counterEvidence: Expert ecological advice does not replace equal voting. Some direct-democracy mechanisms are applications rather than prescribed Charter institutions.

answers.rationale: Transparent periodic elections are integral to Charter democracy.
Expert rule would replace the equal participation the Charter demands.
Every adult should have an equal vote.
Executive override would undermine participatory lawmaking.
Citizens must be free to join their chosen party in a multiparty system.
Transparency requires opposition scrutiny of public spending.
Rights and accountable government require effective independent legal checks.
Organised labour participates but does not replace universal voting.
Incumbent ideological exclusion contradicts free party choice.
Direct participation supports voters’ ability to reconsider laws with rights safeguards.
Concentrated personal authority contradicts decentralised democracy.
Accountability supports defined removal for abuse.
Leaders cannot suspend electoral accountability for convenience.
Recall is consistent with continuing grassroots control of representation.
Unaccountable national leadership violates participatory democracy.
The military cannot substitute its judgement for elected civilian institutions.

axes.brief: Universal rights and bodily integrity protect freedom; public regulation is justified to prevent harm rather than suppress dissent.
axes.counterEvidence: Environmental responsibility requires real regulation; this does not justify indefinite detention or suppression of unpopular protest.

answers.rationale: Bodily autonomy supports self-regarding choice with harm-reduction care.
Serious-crime needs and privacy require narrowly justified oversight.
Peaceful direct action needs protection despite limited disruption.
Free expression protects criticism of public authorities.
Health protection matters but purely paternalistic coercion conflicts with bodily autonomy.
Indiscriminate long-term tracking undermines protected liberties.
Preventing injury to others can justify proportionate road-safety checks.
Concrete threats may justify limited restrictions with strong rights safeguards.
Official moral disapproval is not sufficient grounds for censorship.
Privacy supports communication without blanket government identity checks.
Broad suspicionless searches risk discriminatory and arbitrary interference.
Genuine threats can justify narrow measures but not general suppression of assembly.
Judicial warrants protect against arbitrary interference with the home.
Transparent government requires protection for exposing misconduct.
Nonviolence and reducing interpersonal harm support stronger firearm controls.
Arbitrary indefinite detention contradicts the Charter’s universal rights commitments.

axes.brief: Respect for cultural, linguistic, Indigenous and religious diversity is a founding principle bounded by individual rights.
axes.counterEvidence: The Charter opposes harmful traditional practices as well as discrimination. Cultural accommodation cannot automatically override bodily integrity.

answers.rationale: Cultural diversity should not be overridden automatically by majority identity.
Equal participation justifies practical accommodation.
Migrants need not adopt all majority customs to belong.
Cultural identity can remain distinct within common citizenship.
Linguistic minority rights justify meaningful multilingual access.
Indigenous recognition is explicit in the Charter.
Cultural support should reflect diversity rather than predominantly majority traditions.
Cultural plurality and equal individual rights constrain each other.
Reasonable accommodation is preferable to one compulsory cultural timetable.
Multiple traditions should be recognised within shared national life.
Shared civic participation is valuable without requiring uniformity.
Local multilingual signage supports linguistic inclusion.
Shared citizenship should not require community identity to become secondary.
Religious freedom supports accommodation, but equal safety rules may justify limits.
Diverse cultural ways of life are explicitly valued.
Integration should preserve meaningful cultural choice.

axes.brief: Refugee protection and equal rights support inclusion, while ecological and social capacity remain legitimate planning concerns.
axes.counterEvidence: The Charter prohibits collective expulsion but does not promise that every person in irregular status must remain. Neutral on blanket regularisation is therefore substantive.

answers.rationale: Capacity planning is legitimate but strict quotas require rights and refugee exceptions.
Human dignity generally supports migration for a better life.
Skills-only admission excludes legitimate family and humanitarian reasons.
Family formation is a protected human interest.
Refugees should not be filtered by cultural fit or economic skill.
Fair individual procedures and protection against collective expulsion do not require blanket regularisation.
Employers’ demand is one consideration among rights and ecological capacity.
Housing constraints require investment and planning rather than automatic exclusion.
Rigid family quotas can frustrate basic family rights.
A genuine job offer normally supports admission under fair rules.
Independent humanitarian and personal routes should remain open.
Education is relevant to settlement but not an unconditional guarantee.
Protection from persecution must survive ordinary admission limits.
Cultural-origin preference contradicts equality and diversity.
Resident migrants should share access to essential social provision.
Difference can enrich society without itself establishing preferential admission.

axes.brief: Nonviolence and disarmament are central, but Charter 9.1 permits last-resort UN-mandated force against massive rights violations.
axes.counterEvidence: The express last-resort humanitarian exception rules out absolute pacifism and an only-self-defence rule.

answers.rationale: National advantage alone cannot justify war.
Nonviolent conflict resolution should take priority.
Competitive military superiority contradicts disarmament and common security.
Even imminence requires exceptional necessity and multilateral constraints.
The Charter permits humanitarian force beyond defence but rejects general interventionism.
Compulsory militarisation conflicts with the nonviolent security direction.
Serious concessions can be warranted to avert war.
Autonomous attacks undermine human accountability and restraint.
Defensive protection is preferable to national expeditionary campaigns.
Last-resort protection from genocide is an express exception to absolute avoidance.
Standing overseas combat capacity is lower priority than collective peacekeeping.
Territorial disputes should not be settled by starting wars.
Military threats undermine nonviolent conflict resolution.
Preventing war outweighs national demonstrations of resolve.
Escalatory espionage sits uneasily with cooperative security.
Negotiated arms reductions are central to disarmament.

axes.brief: Global environmental authority, international criminal accountability and strengthened UN cooperation qualify national sovereignty.
axes.counterEvidence: Criticism of the IMF and WTO is counter-evidence to unconditional deference to existing institutions; reform and democratic accountability are required.

answers.rationale: Shared ecological and human-rights obligations qualify national final authority.
Democratically reformed international bodies can bind governments.
Accepted international courts must have practical authority.
Durable cooperative commitments can constrain unilateral action.
Voluntary membership and binding environmental obligations must be reconciled.
The Charter expressly supports ICC accountability.
Immediate national interests cannot routinely override common ecological responsibilities.
Binding international environmental authority is explicitly proposed.
Common international policies are compatible with global action.
Universal-rights commitments can require national legal changes.
Currency sovereignty is conditional on democratic and ecological policy capacity.
Shared resources and authority are necessary for global problems.
Cooperative migration responsibility can qualify exclusive national control.
Common trade rules are acceptable when subordinate to sustainability and rights.
A democratic federation may help, but no single global constitutional form is required.
Upholding legitimate common rules can warrant national costs.

axes.brief: Essential resources such as water should be publicly owned; community entrepreneurship and regulated markets remain legitimate.
axes.counterEvidence: The Charter does not demand nationalisation of all firms. Public water ownership and civic enterprise must both be represented.

answers.rationale: Community enterprise and public essentials imply a mixed ownership system.
Public water and essential networks are explicit commitments.
Democratic and ecological control can justify public ownership even at comparable cost.
Public firms can advance ecological transition in competitive sectors.
Public health is a social good rather than normally a privately owned commodity.
Public transport networks support shared low-impact mobility.
Cost savings matter only alongside labour, ecological and accountability conditions.
Public finance can support sustainable community investment.
Selling public firms is not a general objective independent of social purpose.
Social housing can protect equitable access and sustainable urban planning.
Regulation can suffice in some cases while common strategic control can justify ownership.
Common resource stewardship can justify public extraction ownership where extraction is sustainable.
Direct and contracted waste services should be judged by accountability and ecological outcomes.
Strategic social purpose can outweigh immediate sale revenue.
Financial failure requires assessing public purpose and reform before sale.
Public broadcasting can protect accessible information outside commercial concentration.

axes.brief: Trade must be subordinate to ecological and labour standards, with preference for viable local production and resistance to destructive agreements.
axes.counterEvidence: Local sourcing is ecological and social rather than nationality-based; a cheaper foreign low-impact supplier can be preferable.

answers.rationale: Ecological safeguards can justify restrictions, mere domestic commercial protection cannot.
Trade liberalisation must not override local sustainability or labour rights.
Local sourcing can reduce transport damage when genuinely more sustainable.
Lowest commercial terms alone ignore ecological and social costs.
Local essential resilience can justify selective import safeguards.
Unilateral removal is inappropriate where sustainability safeguards would disappear.
Temporary support can establish sustainable local production.
Equal treatment is desirable only within ecological and community-control constraints.
Local sustainable food capacity can justify agricultural safeguards.
Communities should not be forced into destructive competition without protection.
Retaliatory tariffs lack the required ecological or social purpose by themselves.
Equivalent products should face comparable environmental and product taxes.
Harmful subsidies warrant challenge, beneficial foreign green support does not.
Increased dependence is not justified solely by reducing tariffs.
Community stewardship can justify screening foreign strategic acquisition.
Digital access should generally cross borders subject to common environmental and rights standards.

axes.brief: Public ecological steering, investment and prices reflecting environmental costs coexist with community enterprise and informed consumption.
axes.counterEvidence: Environmental-cost pricing and civic enterprise counter a pure command-economy interpretation.

answers.rationale: Enterprise can choose output within binding ecological and social limits.
Sector targets may aid transition but universal compulsory production is not prescribed.
Market prices are useful only after environmental and social costs are incorporated.
Public investment should deliberately steer sustainable development.
Demand alone should not override ecological limits and community needs.
Essential affordability can justify controls with conservation safeguards.
Civic entrepreneurship generally merits entry subject to ecological standards.
Credit can be directed toward sustainable development priorities.
Uncontrolled speculative flows conflict with the proposed financial-transaction controls.
Ecological transition warrants selected public financial support.
Community financial experimentation may help, unregulated private money can undermine accountability.
Fair remuneration supports an effective wage floor.
Free collective bargaining is supported within shared rights.
Monetary policy should support ecological and social goals rather than financial returns alone.
Equitable shelter can justify controls on speculative market rents.
Transition planning is necessary without prescribing routine government direction of every product.

axes.brief: Equitable distribution and unconditional basic needs support progressive fiscal redistribution and participation beyond subsistence.
axes.counterEvidence: Fiscal incentives and entrepreneurship remain part of the Charter; redistribution need not equalise every outcome.

answers.rationale: The Charter seeks to close gaps within and between societies.
Excessive income inequality is itself a legitimate fiscal concern.
Unconditional basic needs justify stronger public support.
Social development requires more than a minimal survival floor.
Greater ability to contribute warrants progressive income taxation.
Shared equitable provision ordinarily outweighs additional affluent retention.
Taxing large inheritances can counter unequal access to resources.
Basic needs should not cease to count after a fixed time limit.
Wealth transfers can support equitable access and common development.
Benefits should respond to need rather than be minimised for taxpayers.
Social participation is part of full human development.
Broad tax cuts should not outrank adequate support for low incomes.
Income supplements can improve fairness alongside decent wage rules.
Uniform marginal rates need not reflect unequal capacity or ecological burden.
Compensated land reform can widen access while protecting community and Indigenous rights.
Equitable opportunity requires provision beyond absolute destitution.

axes.brief: Religious and spiritual diversity is valued, while equal civil rights preclude privileged religious command over government.
axes.counterEvidence: Respect for spiritual traditions does not endorse a state faith, clerical seats or binding religious family courts.

answers.rationale: Universal civil reasons allow religious and nonreligious equality.
One creed should not supply official national law.
Democratic civil government should not require clerical permission.
Religious constitutional privilege conflicts with equal citizenship.
Teaching about diverse beliefs supports respect without coercion.
State faith formation conflicts with spiritual freedom.
Civil law must protect equal rights across religious communities.
Religious officials should not possess a privileged legislative gatekeeping role.
Inclusive official events should avoid state-organised worship.
Public money should support common needs rather than religious adherence.
Neutral public spaces support equal civic inclusion.
Cultural continuity can justify holidays, while explicit religious state endorsement is questionable.
Clerical status should not automatically confer a government seat.
Religious groups should use equal charitable standards rather than extra doctrinal privilege.
Family formation should not require religious approval.
Religious family decisions cannot override equal civil rights and bodily autonomy.

axes.brief: Bodily autonomy, gender equality, same-sex relationship rights and diverse family recognition support substantial social reform.
axes.counterEvidence: The Charter also values Indigenous knowledge and cultural heritage. Reform does not mean erasing all inherited customs.

answers.rationale: Social institutions should adapt to equal rights and changing values.
Tradition cannot outrank equality and bodily autonomy.
Diverse families and forms of cohabitation receive explicit support.
Gender equality opposes imposed conventional sex roles.
Marriage equality is supported in the retrieved Charter.
Recognition should not privilege one household model.
Freedom to control fertility supports early abortion choice.
Children’s access to inclusive information should not be vetoed by traditional expectations.
Equal family rights support adoption without sex-based discrimination.
Cultural respect does not impose one public modesty norm.
Recognition of gender identity supports respectful updated language.
Established morals should be evaluated against equality and freedom.
Equal treatment protects adults in nontraditional gender roles.
Rights reforms need not be delayed solely because institutions are old.
The Charter opposes suppression of LGBT information and supports inclusion.
Harmless cultural heritage can be preserved voluntarily without an overriding obligation.

axes.brief: The precautionary principle explicitly governs uncertain ecological risks; useful sustainable innovation is supported within limits.
axes.counterEvidence: The Council’s 17 June 2024 adoption of the restoration regulation and the Commission’s current implementation page are real acts/context. Their 2030 targets do not prove achieved restoration or ownership by one political tradition. Contemporary implementation check: the Commission reported draft national restoration plans on 1 September 2026, followed by assessment and final plans within one year (restoration-plans). This is a planning milestone under incumbent governments, not proof of restored ecosystems or wholesale adherence to Green doctrine.

answers.rationale: Substantial benefits alone do not overcome uncertain serious long-term ecological risks.
The precautionary principle supports controlled trials pending substantial evidence.
Permanent habitat loss weighs heavily even against useful infrastructure.
Strong medical safety assessment follows precaution and bodily integrity.
Productivity benefits require worker protection and sustainable effects, not automatic adoption.
Intact habitats merit strong priority given ecological limits.
Cultivated-meat benefits require better evidence of environmental consequences.
Irreversible elective implants warrant demanding long-term safety evidence.
The Charter explicitly calls for reduced resource consumption alongside technology.
Poorly understood environmental effects justify delaying major construction.
Minimal safety evidence is inadequate for uncertain irreversible neural enhancement.
Reliability across populations is necessary before broad medical deployment.
Precaution and concern about commodifying life weigh against nontherapeutic embryo enhancement.
The Charter’s GM-crop position is even more restrictive than requiring long-term safety evidence.
Limiting urban sprawl qualifies blanket priority for new infrastructure over undeveloped land.
Avoiding irreversible ecological harm is a central precautionary commitment.

axes.brief: Power should be concentrated locally and regionally, devolved upward only where necessary for cross-border problems and common rights.
axes.counterEvidence: Cross-border environmental authority and national rights standards are explicit limits to isolated local autonomy.

answers.rationale: Local and regional power should be protected wherever effective.
Higher authority should not automatically win competence disputes.
Democratic self-determination supports separation with protection of affected minorities.
Shared ecological and rights programmes may justify limits, but grassroots consent matters.
Regional institutions can reflect local democratic choices.
Distributed policing better fits local accountable institutions.
Local fiscal autonomy must coexist with equitable redistribution.
A common ecological curriculum is supported alongside substantial regional educational control.
Local revenue choices can support accountable self-government.
National labour minimums protect rights while local implementation can vary.
Grassroots control includes meaningful power over local institutional boundaries.
Equal basic healthcare can require common national entitlements.
Indigenous self-determination and institutions are explicit commitments.
Tax competition should not undermine common social and ecological resources.
Locally contained land and wildlife choices belong primarily to regional communities.
Cross-region effects can justify coordination at the necessary higher level.

axes.brief: The Charter stresses education, exclusion and social causes of violence while recognising humans as embodied parts of nature; ecological Nature is not this questionnaire’s heredity pole.
axes.counterEvidence: No biological causal shares are inferred from environmentalism or equal rights. Mixed answers recognise bodily and social influences rather than treating political values as genetic evidence.

answers.rationale: Education and social organisation receive substantial weight in the Charter’s account of conduct.
Equal rights and educational access do not themselves establish a genetic or social majority share of country IQ differences.
Gender-role discrimination and social exclusion support a substantial social explanation.
Ecological and social stressors interact with embodied differences.
Opportunities and education are important in developing interests.
Biological inclinations and learned circumstances can both affect risk-taking.
The Charter deliberately seeks a learned culture of cooperation and peace.
Empathy involves embodied capacities as well as social learning.
Disability and educational conditions both matter to attention, without a fixed causal ranking.
Peace education and cultural change presume significant learned moral responses.
Racism and social insecurity can produce learned perceptions of threat.
Human diversity includes dispositions as well as social formation.
Cultural ideals and embodied responses can jointly shape attraction.
The Charter’s analysis centres social causes of violence rather than a racial biological account.
Education and social opportunity weigh against inherited racial accounts of self-control.
Gender discrimination and unequal opportunity challenge attributing the pay gap mainly to differences in productive economic contribution.

review.notes: Read all 240 answers against the current question wording and checked values, rationales, cited source IDs and axis distinctions. Read the 2017 Global Greens Charter, environmental-ethics scholarship, and current EU implementation material. Confirmed the Charter’s marriage/family equality, secular institutions, precaution, GMO restriction and qualified humanitarian-force exception. Added the 1 September 2026 restoration-plan milestone as implementation context: draft plans and assessment are not achieved ecological outcomes or proof all incumbent coalitions are Green. Preserved mixed ownership and distinct human-trait causation. All answers remain labelled inferred: these are scoped representative models, not claimed questionnaire responses or empirical measurements of adherents. Review used no target scores or similarity tuning. Similarity audit remains the catalogue coordinator’s separate step.
